## Reviewer 1

**Comment 1:** The paper introduces the Truncated Conformal Kalman Filter (TCKF), a forecasting method for censored demand. The method is applied in FPSC, where stockouts and service interruptions prevent true demand from being observed. TCKF combines a Tobit Kalman Filter, which separately models partial and full censorship, with conformal prediction to produce distribution-free prediction intervals and dynamically adjust uncertainty during prolonged censorship. Using both synthetic data and LMIS data from Cˆote d’Ivoire, the study shows that TCKF performs very well compared to many benchmarks, including statistical, machine-learning, and foundational models. A new metric, Inventory Value Added (IVA), demonstrates that TCKF achieves high service levels without overstocking, unlike several alternative approaches. Linking inventory results to public health outcomes, the authors show that TCKF reduces stockout-driven losses in contraceptive access more effectively than competing forecasts. The paper concludes that integrating censored demand estimation with probabilistic forecasting improves both operational reliability and health outcomes in FPSCs.

The manuscript addresses an important yet challenging topic. Demand censoring is widespread across many industries, and properly accounting for it in decision-making can have a substantial impact on a firm’s operational and financial performance. The paper motivates the problem well, and although the empirical focus is on FPSC, the proposed method is general and broadly applicable. Overall, the forecasting component is clearly written and easy to follow. From an analytical standpoint, I recommend several enhancements to improve robustness, as some assumptions appear stringent. The inventory optimization built on top of the forecasts, however, has considerable room for improvement. A wider range of inventory policies could be examined, including the optimal policy as well as heuristics known to perform well in lost-sales settings. In addition, the key evaluation metric could be better aligned with existing literature and practice. I encourage the authors to articulate an economic objective function and evaluate all experiments against this unified criterion. Below, I outline my major comments.

**Response:** Thank you for your careful reading and for summarising the key areas where the manuscript needed strengthening. We agree with your assessment, and your comments were very helpful in improving both the rigor and the practical relevance of the work.

In the revised manuscript, we have addressed each of the issues raised. First, we added a structured robustness analysis to systematically test the main modelling assumptions and clarify when TCKF performs well and when simpler or alternative specifications may be preferable. Second, we strengthened the inventory evaluation by expanding the benchmark set to include additional lost-sales heuristics and an oracle policy based on latent (true) demand, providing a meaningful upper bound for performance comparisons. Third, we revised the inventory evaluation to be guided by a single unified objective function, and we evaluate methods consistently under this criterion.

All changes are incorporated in the main manuscript with supporting details provided in the E-Companion, and the corresponding sections have been updated to improve transparency and interpretability. Given the substantial volume of these revisions, we have opted not to reproduce the entirety of the newly drafted text within this letter. Instead, we kindly invite you to refer to the specific sections referenced under each comment below. We appreciate your constructive feedback, which significantly improved the quality of the paper.

**Comment 2:** Several assumptions require robustness testing. The manuscript relies on a number of modeling assumptions that appear strong, yet their impact on the results is not fully examined (although the authors do test on a real dataset). The gaussian noise and transition dynamics (Eqs 3-4) are a good modeling start, but it is clear that many firms will have different demand patterns. To fully understand the pros and cons of TCKF, I suggest the authors to do a very detailed robustness analysis to showcase when TCKF performs well, and when alternative approaches may be desirable. This would strengthen confidence in the proposed method and clarify which elements of the model are most critical for performance.

**Response:** Thank you for this comment. We agree that a detailed robustness analysis is crucial for fully understanding the boundary conditions and practical applicability of the proposed method. 

To address this, we have introduced a structured robustness analysis in the revised manuscript to systematically examine the sensitivity of TCKF to its key modelling assumptions. We evaluated the following core elements:

- We tested nested structural specifications (local level only, level + seasonality, and the full level–trend–season model). Our diagnostics confirm that for highly intermittent and noisy FPSC demand, introducing excessive structural complexity is counterproductive, and a parsimonious state specification yields equivalent or superior RMSE performance.

- We stress-tested the uncertainty inflation mechanism by sweeping the parameter ($\lambda \in \{0, \hat{\lambda}, 1\}$). The results demonstrate that dynamically estimating $\hat{\lambda}$ maintains robust probabilistic coverage whilst keeping point accuracy stable, justifying our adaptive design over fixed penalty weights.

- We compared global residual pooling against rolling-window calibration. We found that rolling conformal calibration achieves higher empirical coverage without deteriorating RMSE, proving its necessity for adapting to non-stationary forecast errors.

- We mapped TCKF point predictions against actual demand across three operational regimes (normal operations, partial censorship, and full censorship). This clarifies the model's boundary conditions, demonstrating that while the state-space foundation inherently smooths erratic high-demand spikes, explicitly distinguishing between censorship types successfully neutralises the "spiral-down" effect and prevents state collapse.

Together, these diagnostics show which elements of the model are most critical for performance and outline the specific boundary conditions where TCKF excels.

These changes have been incorporated in *Section 3.6*, *Section 3.7*, and *Section 5.7*.

**Comment 3:** The inventory analysis could include stronger benchmarks, including heuristics tailored to lost sales and an oracle policy. The inventory evaluation currently has substantial room for improvement. There exist well-known heuristics that perform better in lost-sales settings (myopic policies, capped base-stock,...), and these could be included as benchmarks. In addition, incorporating an oracle policy, i.e., one that orders using the true (latent) demand, would provide an upper bound against which all methods can be compared. Together, these additions would result in a more meaningful assessment of the value added by the proposed forecasting approach.

**Response:** Thank you for this excellent suggestion. We fully agree that expanding the inventory benchmarks to include dedicated lost-sales heuristics and an Oracle bound provides a significantly more rigorous and meaningful assessment of the operational value added by our forecasting framework. 

To address this, we have substantially overhauled the inventory evaluation layer in the revised manuscript:

- We explicitly formalised the monthly periodic-review lost-sales system with a fixed lead time of one month ($L=1$). Replenishment decisions are now formally based on an inventory-position (on-hand plus pipeline stock) order-up-to structure, accurately reflecting the physical constraints of the replenishment cycle.

- We expanded the policy suite well beyond the original two rules. We now evaluate all forecasting methods under a comprehensive set of replenishment policies. Specifically, we have included uncertainty-aware base-stock policies and myopic lost-sales heuristics commonly used in practice, directly addressing your recommendation.

- We incorporated an Oracle policy that orders using the true latent (uncensored) demand to establish a theoretical performance upper bound. Interestingly, our analysis reveals that even with perfect foresight, the Oracle achieves a Cycle Service Level (CSL) of 0.97 rather than a perfect 1.00 in the numerical setting. This demonstrates that the system remains constrained by physical operational bounds (e.g., the positive lead time and non-negative ordering limits), establishing 0.97 as the true achievable service ceiling for our comparisons.

These changes have been incorporated in *Section 4.2*, *Section 5.4*, and *E-companion, Section 3*.

**Comment 4:** A single economic objective should guide the evaluation. The manuscript introduces a key evaluation metric, but it would benefit from aligning this with a single, well-defined economic objective that reflects the trade-offs faced in practice (ordering cost, holding cost and lost-sales penalties). I recommend formulating such an objective and evaluating all experiments against it. This would unify the analysis, make comparisons across models more interpretable, and bring the study in line with common practice in the inventory and forecasting literature.

**Response:** Thank you for this comment. We agree that the manuscript benefits significantly from aligning the evaluation with a single, well-defined economic objective to make the operational trade-offs explicitly interpretable.

Because exact item-level financial cost parameters (e.g., unit holding and shortage costs) are not available in the LMIS data, and because public health facilities face highly asymmetric opportunity costs, we have introduced the *Unified Relative Score (URS)*. Adapted from [@petropoulos2019], the URS serves as a unified quadratic (L2 norm) cost function that explicitly captures the trade-off between severe service failures (relative stockout rate) and disproportionate inventory accumulation (relative normalised inventory). The adoption of the squared form is a deliberate methodological choice to heavily penalise the extreme operational imbalances, such as the massive inventory hoarding frequently utilised by human planners to manually buffer against stockouts. 

To ensure our conclusions are robust and not driven by a single subjective cost assumption, we evaluate all forecasting methods across a comprehensive grid of shortage penalty weights ($w \in \{0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 0.90\}$). Evaluating all experiments against this single objective clearly unifies the analysis: it demonstrates that while some baselines appear competitive under extreme, isolated weightings, TCKF consistently provides the most robust joint performance across the spectrum of realistic operational constraints.

While the URS now guides the primary economic evaluation, we have retained CSL and $I_{norm}$ as transparent operational metrics, and we utilise the Stock-Out Rate (SOR) specifically to translate these outcomes into downstream public-health impacts (e.g., unintended pregnancies).

These changes have been incorporated in *Section 4.3.3*, *Section 5.4*, *Section 5.5*, and *E-companion, Section 6*.

**Comment 5:** In summary, the manuscript offers a well-motivated and promising approach to censored-demand forecasting, and the empirical results demonstrate the potential value of TCKF; however, several substantive improvements are needed before the contribution is fully convincing. Most importantly, the authors could expand the robustness analysis to systematically test the key modeling assumptions to better understand when TCKF performs well and when it may not. The inventory analysis could also be strengthened by incorporating additional lost-sales heuristics and, critically, an oracle policy based on true latent demand to establish meaningful performance bounds. Finally, the evaluation would benefit from the introduction of a single, well-defined economic objective function (capturing holding, ordering, and lost-sales costs) so that all methods can be compared on a unified basis. Implementing these changes will substantially enhance the rigor, interpretability, and practical relevance of the paper. I recommend a major revision.

**Response:** Thank you for your careful review and constructive feedback. Your comments were very helpful and have significantly improved the rigor, clarity, and practical relevance of the manuscript.
